newsitem.title: FRANCE: Pressure mounts in France over immigration bill.
newsitem.headline: Pressure mounts in France over immigration bill.

text.p: Pressure mounted on the French government on Tuesday to withdraw or amend a fiercely contested immigration bill that would require citizens to report to the police when foreign guests leave their homes.
Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin urged conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe to drop the bill which he said was "despicable" in spirit and "useless" in practice.

"Rather than further toughening laws that turn out never to be effective, we propose concentrating on (attacking) the organisation of illegal labour, which would dry up an important source (of illegal immigration)," Jospin said.
As a politician he could not advocate civil disobedience, but as a "private citizen" he could not imagine reporting to the police if a foreign friend left his home, he said.

The influential, conservative-dominated French Mayors Association said the proposed measure would be ineffective and called for an amendment leaving it solely to the state to check whether foreigners respected the terms of their visas.

The left-wing daily Liberation, which called on Monday for a million protest signatures before the National Assembly gives the bill a second reading next Tuesday, published four pages of names of intellectuals, elected officials and professionals who opposed the legislation or called for civil disobedience.
New petitions sprouted like mushrooms with magistrates, architects and psychologists joining the ranks of protesters.
The 59 film makers who signed the original appeal against Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre's bill last week included several supporters of the centre-right government.
Juppe stood by the bill in a radio interview on Monday, calling it "balanced" and accusing critics of playing into the hands of the extreme-right National Front.
But he left himself an emergency exit, saying it was up to parliament in its wisdom, subject to approval by the Constitutional Council, to make the law.
A senior parliamentarian in Juppe's Gaullist party, Pierre Mazeaud, called a news conference for Wednesday to offer a "solution" to the dispute.
An amendment by Mazeaud, chairman of the parliamentary legislation committee, could get the government off the hook.
Civil rights and anti-racist groups, backed by the left-wing opposition, have called demonstrations for Saturday and next Tuesday, when the bill returns to the National Assembly.
The National Front, which advocates expelling three million immigrants, meanwhile derided the bill as a "half-measure" that showed the government was not serious about halting immigration.

The Front's number two, Bruno Megret, said in a radio interview: "The intellectuals are totally cut off from the people. They all agree with each other in the near-totalitarian conformism which reigns in the French intellectual classes... This is a severe sign of degeneration."
Megret called the bill "a little half-measure which everyone knows will change nothing and shows the government is pursuing a botched policy of half-measures that provoke major opposition".
He said the government should tighten controls on France's borders instead of counting on citizens to do its job.

"We must bring the number of immigrants down below the threshold of tolerance...There are millions who go back to their country of origin every year on holiday. Let them stay there. It's a question of national survival," Megret said.

He said the new National Front city council in Vitrolles, which his wife conquered in an election this month, would sack dozens of "totally ineffective" social workers to create more jobs for the police in the town north of Marseille.
